title: Advanced Firewall Rules with iptables
markdown:
# Advanced Firewall Rules with `iptables`

`ufw` is a clean, user-friendly interface — but underneath every `ufw allow 22` command is a raw `iptables` rule that the kernel actually enforces. Understanding `iptables` directly gives you the ability to write rules that `ufw` cannot express: logging dropped packets with custom prefixes, rate-limiting connection attempts, and building multi-stage filtering pipelines.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/iptables-1.svg)

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Read and interpret `iptables` rule listings
- Add, insert, and delete rules in the `filter` table
- Block and allow traffic by source IP, destination port, and protocol
- Use stateful connection tracking to allow return traffic without opening extra ports
- Persist rules so they survive a reboot

## What We Are Building

The `Poridhi.io` security team needs three firewall controls that `ufw` cannot express:

1. **Stateful filtering** — allow return traffic for existing connections without opening extra ports
2. **Rate limiting** — throttle new SSH connection attempts to block brute-force attacks
3. **Logging** — record every dropped packet with a searchable prefix before discarding it

We will build these step by step, starting from zero and ending with a working, persistent firewall policy.

## Core Concepts

Before writing any rules, here is the vocabulary you need.

`iptables` organises rules into **chains** inside **tables**. Every packet entering or leaving the machine passes through a chain from top to bottom. The first rule that matches wins.

| Concept | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| Table | A group of chains with a common purpose. We work in the `filter` table throughout this lab. |
| Chain | An ordered list of rules. We mainly use the `INPUT` chain — traffic arriving at this host. |
| Rule | A match condition plus a target. Example: match TCP port 22, target ACCEPT. |
| Target | What happens to a matching packet: `ACCEPT`, `DROP`, `REJECT`, or `LOG`. |
| Policy | The default action when no rule matches — `ACCEPT` or `DROP`. |

The four targets behave differently in ways that matter:

- **ACCEPT** — let the packet through.
- **DROP** — silently discard it. The sender gets no response and waits until timeout.
- **REJECT** — discard it and immediately send an ICMP error back to the sender.
- **LOG** — write a log entry and *continue* to the next rule. This is the only non-terminating target.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/iptables-02.svg)

> **Safety note:** `iptables` changes take effect immediately. A misplaced `DROP` rule can lock you out of SSH before you can fix it. We always insert the SSH allow rule first, at position 1, before adding any deny rules.

## Part 1: Reading the Current State

Never touch a firewall without reading it first.

```bash
sudo iptables -L -v -n --line-numbers
```

| Flag | What it shows |
|------|--------------|
| `-L` | List all rules (defaults to the `filter` table) |
| `-v` | Verbose — includes packet/byte counters and interface names |
| `-n` | Numeric — shows raw IPs and ports instead of resolved names |
| `--line-numbers` | Adds a position number to each rule, needed for targeted deletion |

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image.png)

In the Poridhi environment you will see pre-existing rules from **Docker** and **NetBird** (the WireGuard-based VPN the platform uses). You will see chains like `NETBIRD-ACL-INPUT` and `DOCKER-FORWARD` already plugged in. These handle VPN and container traffic — we will add our rules alongside them without touching them.

> **What to look for:** Check the default policy on the `INPUT` chain — it shows as `policy ACCEPT` or `policy DROP` at the top of the chain listing. This is the fallback for any packet that matches no rule.

## Part 2: Installing Required Tools

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y netcat-openbsd iptables-persistent iptables
```

`iptables-persistent` provides the `netfilter-persistent` command, which saves and restores rules across reboots. `netcat-openbsd` gives us the `nc` command for testing ports.

Also start a test HTTP server on port `8080` in a second terminal — we will use it throughout the lab:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8080
```

## Part 3: Basic Rule Management

### Protect SSH first — always

The first rule you add should always protect your SSH session. Insert it at position 1 so it is evaluated before anything else, no matter what deny rules come later:

```bash
sudo iptables -I INPUT 1 -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
```

Verify it landed at position 1:

```bash
sudo iptables -L INPUT -v -n --line-numbers
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image-1.png)

You will see your SSH rule at position 1, with the existing NetBird rules pushed down to positions 2–4.

### Allow port 8080

```bash
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 8080 -j ACCEPT
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image-2.png)

`-A` **appends** to the end of the chain. Use `-A` for rules that are not safety-critical. Use `-I <position>` when order matters.

### DROP vs REJECT — seeing the difference

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/iptables-sequence.svg)

Add a DROP rule for port 23 and use `time` to measure how long the connection takes:

```bash
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j DROP
time nc -z -w 2 localhost 23
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image-3.png)

The command runs for the full 2 seconds before failing — DROP gives the sender nothing to react to, so it waits until timeout. Now swap it for REJECT:

```bash
sudo iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j DROP
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j REJECT
time nc -z -w 2 localhost 23
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image-4.png)

This returns in milliseconds — REJECT sends an immediate ICMP error back. Use DROP when hiding ports from scanners; use REJECT for services that should give clear feedback.

**Clean up:**

```bash
sudo iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j REJECT
```

### Blocking a source IP

To block all traffic from a specific IP:

```bash
sudo iptables -I INPUT 2 -s 192.168.99.100 -j DROP
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image-5.png)

Inserting at position 2 places it after the SSH safety rule but before everything else. Remove it after testing:

```bash
sudo iptables -D INPUT -s 192.168.99.100 -j DROP
```

> **Important:** Always delete rules by their full specification, not by line number. Line numbers shift every time a rule is added or removed, so deleting by number risks removing the wrong rule.

## Part 4: Stateful Connection Tracking

Without stateful filtering, allowing a server to make outbound connections would require opening all high-numbered ports inbound for the responses — a large security hole. **Connection tracking** (`conntrack`) solves this: the kernel tracks every connection and automatically allows return packets for connections it has already seen.

### The four connection states

| State | When it applies |
|-------|----------------|
| `NEW` | The first packet of a connection (e.g. a TCP SYN) |
| `ESTABLISHED` | Subsequent packets in a tracked connection |
| `RELATED` | A new connection that belongs to an established one (e.g. an ICMP error reply) |
| `INVALID` | A packet that doesn't belong to any known connection — usually malformed or a scan |

### Building the stateful chain

Add these three rules. Each uses `-I INPUT 2`, so they push each other down as they are inserted — the comment on each line shows where it ends up:

```bash
# Ends up at position 4 — discard malformed packets early
sudo iptables -I INPUT 2 -m conntrack --ctstate INVALID -j DROP

# Ends up at position 2 — allow all return traffic for existing connections
sudo iptables -I INPUT 2 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# Appended at the end — allow ping
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p icmp -j ACCEPT
```

Check the result:

```bash
sudo iptables -L INPUT -v -n --line-numbers
```

The chain should look like this:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image-6.png)

Rules 1–3 and 7–8 are ours. Rules 4–6 are NetBird's VPN rules — they only match traffic on the `wt0` interface and don't affect general traffic.

### Testing it
 
Make an HTTP request to the local test server and confirm a response comes back:
 
```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8080 -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n"
```
 
Expected output: `200`
 
Now, inspect the chain:
 
```bash
sudo iptables -L INPUT -v -n --line-numbers
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image-7.png)
 
You should see two counters increment:
 
- **Rule 7** (port 8080 ACCEPT) increments by 1 — the outgoing SYN was matched here, confirming the new connection hit our ACCEPT rule.
- **Rule 2** (ESTABLISHED,RELATED) increments noticeably — the response packets from the server matched the conntrack rule, confirming it is actively handling return traffic.
 
This is the correct way to verify any firewall rule — don't assume it works, watch the counter move.

### Viewing tracked connections

```bash
sudo conntrack -L
```

If `conntrack` is not installed:

```bash
sudo cat /proc/net/nf_conntrack | head -5
```

Each entry shows two address pairs — the **original direction** and the **reply direction**. For example:

```
tcp  6  TIME_WAIT src=127.0.0.1 dst=127.0.0.1 sport=54312 dport=8080
                  src=127.0.0.1 dst=127.0.0.1 sport=8080  dport=54312 [ASSURED]
```

The first line is the outgoing connection; the second is the return path the kernel maps responses back through. You will also see NetBird, SSH, and other system connections — `conntrack -L` shows the full connection table for the host.

## Part 5: Rate Limiting SSH

The `limit` match extension lets you cap how many times a rule can match per unit of time. Applied to SSH, it throttles brute-force login attempts at the kernel level — before they ever reach the SSH daemon.

### The approach

We replace the single plain SSH `ACCEPT` rule with two rules:

- **Existing sessions** (`ESTABLISHED`) — always accepted, no rate limit. Your current terminal session is never interrupted.
- **New connections** (`NEW`) — rate-limited to 5 per minute with an initial burst of 10.

### Step 1: Remove the plain SSH rule

```bash
sudo iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
```

### Step 2: Add the two replacement rules

Insert the `NEW` rate-limited rule first, then insert the `ESTABLISHED` rule at position 1 — this pushes `NEW` to position 2, which is exactly where we want it:

```bash
# Insert at position 1 — will be pushed to position 2 by the next command
sudo iptables -I INPUT 1 -p tcp --dport 22 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW \
  -m limit --limit 5/min --limit-burst 10 -j ACCEPT

# Insert at position 1 — existing sessions, no rate limit
sudo iptables -I INPUT 1 -p tcp --dport 22 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
```

Verify the result:

```bash
sudo iptables -L INPUT -v -n --line-numbers
```

The top of the chain should now look like this:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image-8.png)

Your active SSH session matches rule 1 and is always accepted. A brute-force tool hammering new connections hits rule 2 and gets throttled to 5 attempts per minute after the initial burst of 10.

## Part 6: Logging Dropped Packets

`LOG` is the only non-terminating target in `iptables` — it writes a kernel log entry and then **passes the packet to the next rule** rather than stopping. This means you can place a `LOG` rule immediately before a `DROP` rule to get an auditable record of every blocked packet.

### Add LOG + DROP for port 23

```bash
# Log the packet first
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j LOG --log-prefix "IPT-DROP-TELNET: " --log-level 4

# Then drop it
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j DROP
```

`--log-prefix` sets a searchable label on every log entry. `--log-level 4` is syslog `warning` priority — the standard level for firewall drops.

### Trigger the rule and check the log

```bash
nc -z -w 1 localhost 23
```

```bash
sudo dmesg | grep "IPT-DROP-TELNET" | tail -5
```

You should see something like:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image-9.png)

`IN=lo` appears because we tested with `localhost` — the loopback interface. On a real server blocking external traffic you would see `IN=eth0`.

## Part 7: Persisting Rules

`iptables` rules live only in kernel memory. A reboot wipes them. `netfilter-persistent` solves this by saving rules to disk and restoring them at boot via `systemd`, before any network interface comes up.

### Save the current rules

```bash
sudo netfilter-persistent save
```

This writes your rules to two files:

- `/etc/iptables/rules.v4` — IPv4 rules
- `/etc/iptables/rules.v6` — IPv6 rules

### View what was saved

```bash
sudo cat /etc/iptables/rules.v4
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2019/images/image-10.png)

The file uses `iptables-save` format — each line starting with `-A` is an append command that will be replayed on restore. You will see all of our rules alongside the pre-existing Docker and NetBird rules. This is expected.

### Restore rules without rebooting

```bash
sudo netfilter-persistent reload
```

Or directly:

```bash
sudo iptables-restore < /etc/iptables/rules.v4
```

## Conclusion

You started with a live system running Docker and NetBird rules you didn't write, and built a working layered firewall policy on top of it without breaking anything. The key skills you practiced — inserting rules at specific positions, using conntrack to handle return traffic, rate-limiting by connection state, and logging before dropping — are the same techniques used in production Linux firewalls, container networking, and cloud security groups.
